r:meetup-2024-07: Hosted at Cisco Meraki, this July 2024 SF Bay Area Ruby Meetup runs five talks: Liz Heym rides time-series data, Lukas Fittl of pganalyze tunes Postgres queries for Rails developers, and Yang Chung self-hosts with Dokku in place of Heroku. Cameron Dutro of GitHub writes a Ruby C extension live, and James Kerr borrows React's ideas to build dynamic Rails forms.
r:meetup-2024-09: GitHub HQ hosted September's SF Bay Area Ruby Meetup, where Cameron Dutro broke down how GitHub ships Web Components and Takashi Kokubun made the case for turning YJIT on in production. Brad Gessler demoed Terminalwire for shipping a CLI straight from your web app, Kamil Nicieja surveyed Rails architectures in the wild, and Konstantin Gredeskoul mapped Ruby 3.3's fibers and ractors.
r:meetup-2024-10: October's SF Bay Area Ruby Meetup at Chime HQ runs three talks: Noel Rappin (Chime) reframes Ruby's ecosystem as one vast legacy codebase, drawn from revising the Pickaxe book; Vladimir Dementyev (Evil Martians) builds a multistep wizard form with form objects and ActiveModel; and Brandon Weaver (One Medical) previews his RubyConf keynote, teaching functional composition through a lemur fable.
r:meetup-2024-11: Four talks span the Ruby stack: Konstantin Gredeskoul (Academia.edu) reaches past packwerk and Rails engines for loose coupling through dependency inversion and pub/sub; Chris Fung (Binti) localizes a Rails app into 21 languages with the i18n-tasks gem; Brad Gessler (Rocketship) embeds content management in Rails via Sitepress; and Jeremy Evans marks ten years and 125 releases of Roda, the hierarchical router behind Ubicloud.
r:meetup-2024-12: Five talks map Ruby's AI surface: Tillman Elser (Sentry) merges duplicate issues with embeddings and PG vector on the Ruby SDK, Justin Bowen unveils the ActiveAgent framework, and Edoardo Serra (Stepful) grades thousands of student submissions on Rails. Kamil Nicieja (Plane) demos the lightweight Lammy gem, and Irina Nazarova (Evil Martians) builds a live voice app with AnyCable, Twilio, and OpenAI.
r:meetup-2025-01: The January 2025 SF Ruby Meetup at Productboard HQ packs four talks: Jason Swett reframes tests as executable specifications built to be read; Bart Agapinan (ID.me) wires WebAuthn passkeys into a Rails sign-in flow with the webauthn gem; Cameron Dutro (GitHub) compiles Ruby's Onigmo regex engine to Wasm and calls it from Ruby via wasmtime; and Alex Rodionov (Toptal) champions Bazel for massive monorepos.
r:meetup-2025-02: GitHub's February SF Ruby meetup packs four talks into one night: Joel Hawksley traces five years of ViewComponent-driven UI architecture at GitHub, Sam Poder explains how Hack Club built a real bank on Rails, Vladimir Dementyev (Evil Martians) probes the edges of real-time presence tracking, and Alan Ridlehoover brings hexagonal architecture to Rails. A practical tour through Ruby running production at scale.
r:meetup-2025-04: April's Sentry-hosted meetup packs five talks: Neil Manvar debugs Ruby errors in record time with Sentry, Rich Steinmetz of ClickFunnels keeps devs focused while scaling an API-integration suite, Jake Zimmerman revisits Sorbet's syntax for Stripe, Todd Sedano bootstraps a Rails project with Packwerk at Gusto, and Irina Nazarova closes on why startups still ship on Rails.
r:meetup-2025-05: Four talks span the Ruby stack: Fito von Zastrow and Alan Ridlehoover unpack how Cisco Meraki decouples its 20-year Rails monolith from Rails constructs, and Obie Fernandez open-sources Shopify's Roast, which threads deterministic steps through LLM calls in YAML-defined AI workflows. Todd Kummer ships a hobby app on Rails 8 and Kamal, and Brandon Weaver turns monads and functors into a fable with Red in Fantasyland.
r:meetup-2025-06: Chime's June meetup runs four talks: Charles Oliver Nutter shows JRuby 10 reaching Ruby 3.4 compatibility and 217 million object allocations per second on the JVM; Melvyn Peignon analyzes 200 billion RubyGems download rows in ClickHouse; Kieran Klaassen brings evaluation-driven development to Rails with his Leva gem; and Justin Bowen maps AI agents onto MVC with Active Agent, treating agents as controllers.
r:meetup-2025-06-elixir: José Valim, Elixir's creator, walks SF Ruby and Elixir builders through Livebook, his Jupyter-style notebook, then unveils Tidewave: an AI coding assistant that runs inside your Rails or Phoenix app rather than scanning files as text. Its open-source MCP server lets agents query the live database, routes, and runtime; a paid page-intelligence layer edits the rendered page straight from clicks.
r:meetup-2025-07: Three talks from a full Figma-hosted meetup: Harrison Touw shows how Figma builds internal admin tools with a Ruby DSL that renders declarative panels, no React scaffolding required; Marco Roth unveils Herb, an HTML+ERB parser powering formatters, linters, and a language server for the Rails view layer; and Jeremy Evans walks through eliminating unnecessary implicit allocations in Ruby.
r:meetup-2025-08: GitHub HQ hosts five Ruby talks: Drew Hoskins demos Temporal's new official Ruby SDK for durable execution, Enrique Mogollán builds an MCP inspector in Ruby, and Miles Georgi unveils Foobara's command-centric framework. Irina Nazarova halves Whop's CI time with test_prof, and Sergey Karayev shows how Superconductor parallelizes AI coding agents across Rails apps.
r:meetup-2025-10: Five Rubyists take the stage at AngelList's Founders Cafe: Chamod Gamage 10x's AngelList's Excel reporting with a graph-based Ruby DSL, Dr. Chris Fung binds Ruby to the Fjall embedded key-value store through a Rust native extension, Scott Motte traces .env files to dotenvx's encrypted, commit-safe secrets, Cameron Dutro debuts LiveComponent for Rails, and Miles Georgi wires AI-backed domain logic into Foobara.
r:meetup-2025-12: Noel Rappin (Chime) tours Ruby 4.0's headline changes: redesigned Ractor ports for true parallelism, experimental Ruby boxes for isolated namespaces, the new ZJIT compiler, and Bundler 4's stricter, more predictable CLI. Justin Bowen then live-demos ActiveAgent v1, wiring AI writing assistants and a Capybara-driven research agent into open-source forks of Writebook and Fizzy.
r:meetup-2026-01: Hosted at Persona, January's meetup runs four talks. Samuel Giddins hunts allocation hotspots in a 10,000-request-per-second Rails monolith, freezing strings and shipping the Arctic gem for frozen ENV lookups; Enrique Mogollán monkey-patches NilClass to trace nil bugs; Vitor Oliveira tours Ruby 4.0's ZJIT, Ruby namespaces, and Ractors; and Todd Kummer customizes Rails form builders for a Stimulus date picker.
r:meetup-2026-02: From the February meetup at Sentry: Sohil Kshirsagar (Tusk) makes the case that coding agents need a harness, not just guardrails, feeding them real context like read-only database access; Mike Dalton demos Calendar Vision, a Hotwire Native app that turns a flyer photo into a calendar event; and Vladimir Dementyev (Evil Martians) asks whether architecture still matters when AI writes the code.
r:meetup-2026-04: Three talks chart Ruby's AI frontier: Brian Scanlan shows how Intercom doubled engineering throughput in nine months on Claude Code, auto-approving 17.6% of pull requests against its Rails monolith. Konstantin Gredeskoul's InquireX gems express adaptive intake forms as typed Ruby DSLs that LLMs pre-fill from free text. Dmitry Kozlov's claude-yolo runs parallel Claude Code agents in tmux with worktree conflict resolution.
v:--PvuOaxVVE: Uscreen bootstrapped for ten years on a single Rails monorepo, and Nick Savrov keeps it deliberately lean: most of the admin runs on Stimulus controllers, hewing close to the Rails starter pack. He even shipped 800 mobile apps built in Rails on Turbolinks across the App Store before moving to Flutter. That discipline helped Uscreen generate nearly a billion dollars for creators ahead of its $150M raise.
v:-H1GZjECTsU: Cisco Meraki's dashboard grew to over 5 million lines of Ruby, and Fito von Zastrow and Alan Ridlehoover scaled it by decoupling business logic from Rails. They extract fat controllers, ERB views, and models into plain Ruby objects inside owned domain namespaces, letting teams move without org-wide consensus. The payoff: test coverage in the domain folder hit 97 percent and method complexity dropped 30 percent.
v:-x9Ir3FakDY: Onboarding onto a thousand-model Rails monolith shouldn't take three months. Brandon Weaver wires MCP tools into Rails introspection and Packwork, demoing a Packwork-ified Mastodon fork where an agent answers what your team owns, traces a URL to its controller and model, and measures a change's blast radius across packs and teams, compressing ramp-up to two or three weeks.
v:1BNBOQOY-58: Ruby on Rails has powered Y Combinator startups since the early days: the founders building companies all shipped on Rails and ran on Heroku, which grew fast and was funded by YC in 2008. This Evil Martians and YC session revisits that lineage and speed-builds a working Rails app live in under ten minutes.
v:21hf1Ue1o6I: NexHealth syncs the patient data trapped in legacy EHRs (cloud and on-prem alike) into a Rails backend, then exposes it through one universal API so developers can finally build on healthcare records. Matt Duszynski demos booking an appointment that lands on the practice's calendar in real time, and shows the platform, powered by Rails, Sidekiq, and Karafka, now spanning 16,269 practices across all 50 states, Canada, and US territories.
v:2h2XEyOM6lg: André Arko distills 20 years of watching Rails apps break into one operating principle: confidence. He maps everything after the deploy onto five categories, errors, data, speed, security, and lead time, pairing each with concrete tools: Honeybadger or Sentry for exception and uptime monitoring, OpenTelemetry traces through Honeycomb, strong_migrations for the three-deploy data dance, rack-mini-profiler and a Fastly CDN for speed, and DORA's finding that the fastest, most frequent deployers ship the fewest failures.
v:3s6Je3wTXqE: Evgeny Li builds a customer-support AI agent live on stage with no slides, wiring Postgres, Notion, Google Docs, and Gmail into one queryable layer. He defines SQL-backed tools, writes the agent's instructions in plain English, and watches Bemi AI handle an inbound email: it runs a semantic search, pulls the customer's subscription, and drafts a reply with the right IPs and plan details.
v:3u72MBYDRFA: Enrique Carlos Mogollán builds an MCP inspector in Ruby, a Postman-style debugger for the Model Context Protocol that ships as both a Thor CLI and a mountable Rails engine. Reusing fast-mcp, the Ruby MCP client, and Faraday over a transport/data/presentation split, it lists and executes tools, then renders live forms via MCP UI and even prompts Claude Code to generate agent skills from a server.
v:4H5V6gnG9Oo: Sidekiq has thrived for 13 years on an open-core model: open source at its heart, with Pro and Enterprise tiers funding decades of maintenance, reaching 2,300 customers and mid-eight-figure revenue on zero outside investment. Mike Perham traces that journey, wrestles with succession and community governance, and announces the Gem Fellowship, $100,000 in annual grants for Ruby open source.
v:5MepvHfFXgk: Fin, Intercom's customer-service AI agent, runs support like software you build, test, and deploy: Ryan Sherlock walks a damaged-order claim through multimodal task flows that read photos, pause for side questions, cite help articles, and translate between an English agent and a Spanish customer in real time. A copilot surfaces internal policies and past resolutions, and teams pay only per resolution.
v:7M4dzK9wY7I: Bart de Water demos Thatch, walking through how an employer funds an ICHRA, an individual coverage health reimbursement arrangement, in about six minutes. Instead of one-size-fits-all group plans, a smart-allowance algorithm sizes each employee's budget by location and dependents, then employees pick their own plans, spending leftover dollars in a marketplace on qualified expenses like Oura rings or digestive health tests.
v:931PpANN8bs: AngelList runs its entire venture-finance platform, more than $15.4 billion invested across 28,000+ startups, on a single Rails monolith. Chamod Gamage demos how the team lifted accountants' Excel-formula "checks" into the reporting stack: their open-source Saxel gem compiles a directed graph into a workbook, an Excel cloud API executes the formulas, and LLM-parsed fund documents flag discrepancies, generating statements nightly for thousands of funds.
v:9Ij63xgLHE4: Paweł Strzałkowski of Visuality turns any Rails app into an AI interface using the official Ruby MCP SDK and a single app template: scaffold a model and you get ten Model Context Protocol tools for every CRUD action out of the box. He wires Claude Desktop to a greenfield review app, 37signals' Campfire, and an Avo app, chaining all three over MCP, then closes the production gap with Doorkeeper OAuth (DCR and PKCE).
v:A3smrePJj4M: Multiwoven is the open-source reverse ETL platform Nagendra Hassan Dhanakeerthi and team built to push data out of warehouses like Snowflake and Databricks into business tools like Salesforce. A Rails control panel plus pluggable Sidekiq or Temporal workers move data through four Active Record models: source, model, sync, destination. Self-hosted on Docker or Kubernetes, it has earned 1.7K GitHub stars.
v:AFpbFXPBs3w: Adrian Marin maps the full Rails asset landscape, retiring Sprockets for Propshaft and walking from the lowest-effort setup (import maps, no build step) up through esbuild bundling and a published npm package for gem authors. Drawing on Avo and the Marksmith editor, he shows how a gem can ship JavaScript so users get fresh assets on a plain bundle update, plus middleware tricks for node-free apps.
v:Bl7Dq6aYidE: Simple AI builds voice agents that answer hundreds of thousands of sales calls daily, replying in under 700 milliseconds, all on Ruby on Rails. Zach Kamran demos the agent builder and its simulation feature, where two AIs phone each other over WebRTC to stress-test a flow. A custom Ruby class turns structured-output fields into OpenAI schemas, while Sidekiq runs the simulations behind the scenes.
v:Cq4sWAf-d5U: Tia Anderson built Palm, a Rails journaling and gardening app, after a layoff, proving she could write Ruby and ship it. She keeps it to roughly 15 well-named models rather than padding to 145, arguing that readable code, breadcrumbs over a maze, is kindness to the maintainer. She wires OpenAI into Palm to generate reflection prompts, imagining AI that escalates to 988 when someone is spiraling.
v:E-NJ-NhY5dk: Eddie Kim co-founded Gusto on Rails in 2012 because it let him move fastest, the one quality he ranks above strategy or fundraising for a startup. Today Gusto runs a 10-million-line Rails monolith with hundreds of developers, scaling it with Packwork rather than rewriting, and Kim still reaches for Devise the moment authentication comes up.
v:ExICQ7RDT0E: Terminalwire ships a command-line app for your web application the way Hotwire ships HTML, streaming standard IO over encrypted WebSockets so the client never updates. Brad Gessler installs it into Rails as an `app/terminal` folder, deploying the CLI to the server itself; one founder shipped a working CLI, then MFA, in five days without users updating a thing. Plane found it burns fewer tokens than MCP for AI integration.
v:F6dwuKszqWs: André Arko demos rv, an open-source Ruby version manager written in Rust and inspired by Python's uv. It ships statically linked, precompiled Rubies that install in roughly one second, immune to the OpenSSL breakage that plagues traditional builds, with shell integration that auto-switches versions like rbenv or chruby. Version 0.2 covers every Ruby across Intel and ARM on macOS and Linux.
v:FDHtRONY4kk: Andy Wang demos Finta, the books-and-taxes platform he founded, turning QuickBooks' 15-minute, row-by-row chore of spreading an annual expense across 12 months into a single click rendered snappily with Rails view components. Finta auto-categorizes 99.7% of transactions at 97% accuracy, hides journal entries and debits behind plain numbers like cash, burn, and runway, and grew revenue 3x yearly to nearly $1M, profitable, on a five-person team.
v:FIipSavS5qo: Ben Sheldon makes the case that performance starts on your laptop, not in production, and the one principle is to load less code. As author of the Good Job gem and former lead of GitHub's Ruby architecture team, he traces a 9-second Rails boot to 4 seconds of needlessly loaded controllers, then shows how separating configuration from behavior, leaning on Zeitwerk autoloading, lazy-load hooks, and Vernier flame graphs keeps development booting fast.
v:FNWAKyTX4Uo: Cora, the AI email assistant Kieran Klaassen built solo on Rails, scans your inbox, briefs the 80% of mail you can skip twice a day, and leaves what matters. Powered by RubyLLM and his own Leva evaluations framework, it serves thousands of users, handles millions of emails, and embodies his "compounding engineering" practice: plan, hand off to AI, review, then codify every learning.
v:Fx-AgNTMIRU: Ruby's edge over Laravel and JavaScript isn't a feature, it's the builders, dreamers, and sponsors who showed up. Irina Nazarova closes SF Ruby Conference 2025 with gratitude to the sponsors, speakers, and volunteers who took a leap of faith on a first-time event, and a reminder that two sponsors, Chime and Gusto, IPOed this year. Ruby remains a powerful force in entrepreneurship, and the community builds on, no permission required.
v:GoFbMl3TBmw: Stepful trains healthcare workers at scale, and Wyatt Ades shows why blanket-grading practice videos through an LLM fails: average error runs 18 out of 100. Measuring error per rubric item exposes one complex objective dragging accuracy down, so flagging it automates 80% of grading and routes the nuanced 20% to human instructors, with tool calls timestamping each objective.
v:H0XwqkQfiIM: Carmine Paolino builds Chat with Work, an AI workplace search tool that skips the heavyweight index-everything approach: instead of synchronizing your entire Google Drive upfront, it hands the LLM tool calls so the model decides when to search, which documents to retrieve and cache, and whether to read a full file or answer directly. The same agentic engine that powers it gave rise to RubyLLM, his Ruby gem for working with language models.
v:J68QOBLEItY: JP Camara, principal engineer at Wealthbox, builds Google-Docs-style collaboration entirely in Rails by pairing Yjs CRDTs with AnyCable's Go-powered WebSocket server. Where Action Cable's broadcast latency balloons toward five seconds at 10,000 connections, AnyCable holds under a second on a single node, replays history through reliable streams, and routes ephemeral cursor presence via Whisper. Compaction through the Rust-backed Y-RB gem keeps thousands of tiny updates from drowning the database.
v:JmmtO8vChyA: Jeremy Evans rebuilds Ubicloud's command-line interface as a thin client: a sub-100-line Go binary that ships every argument to a gateway endpoint, where all parsing and formatting run in Ruby. New API features reach users the moment they deploy, with no client update, and the same logic powers a web shell prototyped in an hour. His rodish gem brings Roda's routing tree to argument parsing.
v:JvCQgUcQNps: Temporal's open-source durable execution platform now ships a Ruby SDK, letting workflows survive crashes as if they never happened: Tom Wheeler of Temporal Technologies kills a running program mid-count and it resumes at four instead of one. His money-transfer demo shows automatic retries, non-retriable error types, the saga compensation pattern, signals for human-in-the-loop approvals, and live bug fixes redeployed mid-workflow.
v:L7WpwtqHn_g: Herb reimagines ERB as an HTML-aware templating engine, and Marco Roth uses it to rebuild the Rails view layer's missing tooling: a language server, formatter, and linter with over 50 rules that flag duplicate IDs, typos, and accessibility gaps as you type. Written in C for portability across Node, Ruby, and the browser via WebAssembly, it powers ReActionView, bringing in-browser error pages, jump-to-source outlines, and a path toward reactive Rails templates.
v:L91KPH6f_q8: Sixfold builds AI for insurance underwriting, and CTO Brian Moseley shows how its agents turn each carrier's risk-appetite manual into a data model that scores submissions 0 to 5 and writes a narrative of the risk signals it surfaces. In two and a half years the platform ingested 40 million documents, processed a million submissions, and saved underwriters 25,000 hours. He'd build the whole stack in Ruby today, eyeing Ruby LLM for the agent layer now written in Python.
v:LK0CmY72U9w: AccessGrid issues wallet credentials, event tickets, key fobs, coupons, loyalty cards, into Apple, Google, and Samsung wallets through a single API, collapsing what once meant separate deals, multi-region deployments, and a $10,000 certification per platform. Auston Bunsen demos the full flow live: generate an AES-128 key pair, design a pass, then issue a working door key via QR code that an audience volunteer installs on the spot.
v:N5VpMNgbrsg: Reading Rails source rewards active engagement: Kasper Timm Hansen treats the console as a microscope, calling `method(:name)` to jump straight to a definition's source location, then verifying each guess by running fragments live. He traces `extract_options!`, `assert_valid_keys`, and the callback machinery across ActiveModel, ActiveRecord, and ActiveSupport, modeling how to grab one percent of Rails at a time.
v:Nhe8FXbN0p0: Brittany Martin Springer returns to code as engineering manager at Roadrunner Recycling, opening SF Ruby Conference 2025 alongside Irina Nazarova and 400 Rubyists. Their charge: make Ruby and Rails the pragmatic default for new products, learning why startups choose it today and what the ecosystem still needs. Ruby is futureproof, they argue, and optimism is a consequence of our effort: if we build it.
v:Ou7CGuQUy6Q: Recognize runs employee recognition for the enterprise on Ruby on Rails, scaling from Rails 3.2 to 7.1 across 53,000 commits and a 13,000-test suite that finishes in ten minutes. Peter Philips shows how provisioning an 80,000-employee customer buckled under a decade of Active Record callbacks, so his team built an async pub/sub system that fires one event for parallel listeners, now handling up to 500,000 jobs a day.
v:P8myd01GxAA: Superconductor gives every coding agent its own dedicated cloud development environment, so Arjun Singh can launch Claude Code, Codex, and Gemini in parallel on one ticket, then review each from his phone via screenshots and a live running Rails app. Built with Hotwire Native and wired into Slack and GitHub with shared context, it even benchmarks each agent against your own codebase rather than Python-only SWE-bench.
v:Po-k0sddd0Y: Leonardo, the browser-based coding agent from Kody Kendall's LlamaPress, builds Rails apps from a chat prompt: it reads and writes the file system, runs scaffolding and migration commands, and scaffolds a working task tracker live on stage. Built as a "deep agent" like Claude Code, it spins up sub-agents that invoke Rails controllers as tool calls, routing through Devise and CanCan so each agent respects the signed-in user's role.
v:QeC8VfRj-5M:
This is an Open Mic session with multiple speakers, so I'll summarize the collection of lightning demos rather than a single thesis.

Open mic turns the stage over to builders shipping in Ruby: Raul Andreescu demos OG Pilot, a dynamic Open Graph image generator that scrapes a site's branding and lifts click-through up to threefold; another maintainer rallies contributors to the Environmental Data & Governance Initiative's web-monitoring tooling; and Miles Georgi unveils Fubara, a command-centric framework that makes a domain discoverable enough to expose as an MCP, CLI, or auto-generated TypeScript SDK.
v:WItgAAtvJhc: James Kerr demos Tend, the budget app he built and dogfoods, that collapses household finance into a single number: his real weekly discretionary allowance. Modeled on the 1904 Japanese kakeibo method, Tend calendars a year of income and fixed expenses with the ice_cube gem, sets aside special and unexpected costs, then surfaces what's left to spend. Bootstrapped solo on Rails, he just shipped Stripe and landed his first two paying users.
v:WxdB4sg2eIM: Sam Lambert shards a live MySQL database in under ten minutes on PlanetScale, migrating a running "slashrot" app onto an 11-shard Vitess cluster without touching a line of application code. A transparent V-schema hands ID generation to Vitess via a central sequence table, keeps posts and comments on the same shard for in-shard joins, then cuts traffic over fully online. The result: limitless horizontal scale, millions of QPS, what once took years.
v:XBZcLD5xcPY: Inertia Rails glues Rails and React into one monolith, letting each play to its strengths. Brandon Shar, Svyatoslav Kryukov, and Brian Knoles, the adapter's three core maintainers, scaffold a Vite-TypeScript-React app with a single `rails new`, then layer live search, persistent layouts, shared props, and deferred props. Rails drives state and validation while React stays a thin view layer, no GraphQL or client-side routing required.
v:XSdBCKepWHM: ZJIT, the JIT compiler Takashi Kokubun and Shopify's Ruby team are building for Ruby 4.0, compiles whole methods into a Ruby-aware high-level IR, unlocking cross-method optimizations YJIT couldn't reach: it constant-folds 1 plus 2 into a returned 3, guarded by patch points that invalidate on redefinition. With YJIT already doubling RailsBench over the interpreter, ZJIT extends the playbook through type profiling, inlining, and register allocation.
v:Xc8OYnIci3E: Intercom runs a 14-year-old Rails monolith at two million MySQL requests per second, and Eugene Kenny traces the layered scaling techniques that got it there: vertical scaling, per-feature databases, IdentityCache (now absorbing ten million reads per second), read replicas via Makara, and hand-rolled sharding of a 25-billion-row conversations table, before consolidating onto PlanetScale's Vitess for zero-downtime, resharding-on-demand growth.
v:Y_J84x5ePUs: Hack Club's HCB, a fiscal-sponsorship neobank built as a vanilla Rails monolith moving millions for hackathons and mutual-aid groups, took a full year to open-source. Sam Poder details the work: a "Big Scrub" of 5,000 PII-laden issues, rotating every credential and migrating secrets to Doppler, git-filter-repo surgery, and Brakeman plus a bounty program. The payoff: 76 contributors, a #2 Product Hunt launch, and users who watch their feature requests ship.
v:c0v3qj06nfc: Ruby's dynamism is a toolkit. Noel Rappin walks a resume-matching method through four ways to tame type errors without static checks: raise loudly at boundaries, coerce surprises (Kernel's Array() turns nil into an empty list), minimize stray nils, and objectify hashes into Structs or Data objects that own their validation. His sharpest point: a years-versus-days mixup is a type error no static system catches.
v:f20j7Cmq7JI: Active Agent brings AI features into Rails by modeling agents on Action Mailer: prompts render as text.erb views, tools become JSON schema, and structured outputs map straight to Active Record classes. Justin Bowen, drawing on 20 years of Rails, demos browser agents that navigate and screenshot pages plus a streaming writing assistant wired through Turbo Streams with zero JavaScript. The v1 release candidate ships now.
v:gTHmwQviVI8: Sarah Mei argues that a software developer's job has always been to build software systems, not to write code, so AI coding assistants represent the same kind of abstraction jump Ruby developers already survived: virtual machines freed us from manual memory management, the cloud freed us from server closets. Each shift wrote more software, more ambitiously, by more people. The work moves toward orchestration, and the mandate holds.
v:hP4SkKH4IsA: Rails X, a future version of Rails, grows from the whole community: Vladimir Dementyev argues every speaker, contributor, and startup founder already shapes it. Working through four evolution drivers (reflect, listen, observe competitors, predict), he maps the gaps and demos Rails running in-browser via WebAssembly and bolt.new, with gems like callback_hell, Vite Rails, and Action Cable Next.
v:kdVAm_yzqpE: Avinash Joshi demos Cactus, a YC-backed voice AI platform built on Ruby on Rails for home-services businesses like HVAC and plumbing. A live call shows the AI answering as "Pam," triaging a broken-AC emergency, capturing the address and email, then qualifying the lead, summarizing the transcript, and booking the job into the CRM. One HVAC customer added roughly $37,000 in revenue.
v:ltYep_SOjNg: Rachael Wright-Munn mines programming games like Exapunks, One Dreamer, and Battlesnake for developer-experience ideas any Rubyist can steal. She maps their joy onto five levers: immediate feedback via TDD and `binding.b`, live reloading with Jekyll and Vite, color through raw ANSI codes, documentation as starter projects and zines, and the autonomy that makes open source feel like play. Ruby already has the tools; she shows how to make them delightful.
v:nJ6oxetPDMY: Cleary, the AI-powered HR support platform Ryan O'Donnell co-founded and runs on Ruby on Rails, layers a knowledge-base chatbot, agentic workflows, and a self-driving ticketing system. O'Donnell demos live: two-tier classification routes a request, tools match a referral resume to open roles, and a mortgage-letter ticket resolves in 10 seconds. Built-in evals track the 80-85% classification success rate in production.
v:nfeEQBmeirg: Suppli runs $8 billion in open invoices across 70-plus distributors and 20,000 paying customers with a team of six engineers, proof, as CTO David Paluy puts it, that Ruby lets a tiny team carry enormous load. Suppli wraps decades-old ERPs in per-system Ruby adapters, then uses LLM-driven YAML instruction files to spin up new integrations in 33 minutes, turning months of tribal knowledge into an SMS-and-pay flow.
v:py_vjWTmAwg: Stephan Hagemann reframes Packwerk as one tool among many for shaping Rails architecture, not a cure for a tangled monolith. Drawing on retrospectives from Shopify, Eileen Uchitelle, and Brandon, he shows how PKS (a faster Rust implementation) parses every file to catch non-autoloaded dependencies that Zeitwerk misses, while warning that naive privacy fixes manufacture accidental public APIs. The real skill, like wielding a hammer, is learning to draw boundaries yourself.
v:pzA1Q8sBwcA: Bolt.new runs on a Ruby on Rails backend powering authentication, payments, and billing, while StackBlitz's WebContainers execute full-stack apps inside the browser's own CPU. Co-founder and CTO Albert Pai tells Irina Nazarova how seven years of grinding preceded an overnight hit: zero to $20M ARR in a month, $40M within eight weeks, once Claude Sonnet 3.5 made AI codegen reliable.
v:rhmINL-nK5o: Ubicloud is an open-source infrastructure cloud, an alternative to AWS, and Dan Farina deploys a full Mastodon instance on it live: four VMs, managed Postgres, load balancers, and subnets spun up via a dozen CLI commands. He shows how Ubicloud couples firewalls to subnets for performance and uses DNS-based layer-4 load balancers that hand TLS termination back to your instance. It runs on 85,000 lines of Ruby with 100% branch coverage and, remarkably, no Rails.
v:sjuCiIdMe_4: Dave Thomas makes a provocative case: in Ruby, reaching for `class` is a reflex worth breaking. Drawing on years writing Elixir, he argues most classes that hold no state, ship a lone `perform`, subclass an abstract base, or just bucket data should be modules, `Struct`s, `Data`, plain hashes, or freestanding functions. The payoff is real: looser coupling, smaller methods, free polymorphism, and code that's far easier to test and debug.
v:tE_gTgnoLw8: Evgeny Li builds Bemi AI's multi-tenant cloud data infrastructure on plain Ruby, provisioning isolated per-customer stacks that store Postgres logical-replication changes as immutable Parquet files on S3 and query them with DuckDB. He argues Ruby's rich standard library, ERB templating, and shell control make it the best language for scripting and automation, and shows patterns like dry-run, sidecar, GitOps, and idempotent scripts that go off Rails when a monolith won't fit.
v:xP86mvtqEh0: Engineering is a marketing superpower: Colleen Schnettler shows how technical founders win distribution by shipping small free tools that funnel into their product. She built an AI virtual try-on Chrome extension that drove paid signups for Simple File Upload, since the Replicate API it relied on deletes files hourly. Her rule: do outreach by hand 12 times before automating, because the message matters more than the workflow.
v:y535u1EWqAg: RubyLLM gives Ruby developers one clean API across 11 providers and hundreds of models, collapsing LangChain's import-and-initialize ceremony into a single `chat.ask` call. Carmine Paolino extracts the gem from his Chat with Work product and shows a full Rails chat app, persisted to the database with streaming UI, generated in under two minutes. Now past 4 million downloads and 3,200 stars, it proves AI development is product development, and Ruby ships products.
v:ydkP8yB9ozg: José Valim, creator of Elixir and CEO of Tidewave, frames coding agents as model plus instructions plus tools plus runtime, and argues the biggest wins come from owning the runtime. He demos Tidewave embedding that loop in the browser, where it inspects the live page, maps DOM back to Rails templates, builds a chat-search feature, and tests itself until it catches its own bug. His pitch for Ruby: structured templates like Herb and runtime documentation APIs make introspection that serves humans and agents alike.
v:zXbAWkUueUM: Bolt.new packs an entire dev environment into the browser through StackBlitz's WebContainers, a client-side mini operating system that boots Node, bash, and npm in 100-200 milliseconds with no remote VMs to provision. Alex Kalderimis and Albert Pai demo it by generating a full SF Ruby conference site, schedule, auth, a SQL database, and Stripe ticket payments through a webhook, the same way the 2025 conference site was prototyped. Across 6 million users, vibe coding hands every backend engineer a front-end pair.
